newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Pakistan brokers Afghan Taleban talks with warlord.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan brokers Afghan Taleban talks with warlord.

text.p: Afghanistan's ruling Taleban movement began sudden peace talks on Wednesday with powerful northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, Afghan sources said.
Both sides conferred for four hours at a meeting apparently brokered by neighbouring Pakistan and agreed to talk again on Thursday.
The sources said the conference between Dostum and Taleban acting foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghaus was attended by Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar.
Also present was Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction leader Karim Khalili, an ally of the Uzbek general.

The four-hour meeting at Qala-i-Jangi fort outside Mazar-i-Sharif, capital of Balkh province, decided to continue the talks on Thursday on the proposed formation of a commission that should decide about the country's political future, a spokesman for Dostum said.
The meeting was the first known high-level contact between Dostum and the Taleban, whose militia captured the capital Kabul on September 27 ousting President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government.
It was held only two days after Dostum acknowledged Rabbani's legitimacy as president after previously remaining neutral in the fighting between Taleban and the ousted government.
But there has been no evidence so far of Dostum's army joining battles between the Talaban and ousted government forces led by former defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood now raging north of Kabul.

Babar's visit was his second to Mazar-i-Sharif in two days. He earlier came to Dostum's stronghold on Tuesday after talks with Taleban officials in Kabul as part of Pakistan's move to arrange peace talks between the warring sides.
Dostum's spokesman, General Mohamed Youssef, said Thursday's talks would be held at Shibarghan, capital of the neighbouring Jozjan province.
He said the proposed commission should have representation from all Afghan groups.

Pakistan said on Tuesday it was ready to bring the Afghan groups together to resolve their differences peacefully and agree on a broad-based government that could bring durable peace to their war-shattered country.
Rabbani's government has been accusing Islamabad of backing the Taleban, which emerged from Afghan refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago.
Pakistan denies the charge and says it has no favourites among the Afghan factions, most of which it helped during their guerrilla war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
